However, retrofitting an existing floating platform (if it could be proven possible) would be very expensive, and it would disrupt ongoing production operations for months. The existing platform would need to have platform space and load capacity (buoyancy) for the additional electrical equipment, the OTEC refrigerant storage, and the pumps and heat exchangers used in the OTEC system. Some of this equipment may be able to be mounted subsea, but with higher costs and equipment complexity. 4 OESI 2.0 M-1 T-1-P1.1 – Objective 3 Report April 2025 Figure 1: Hull Members of a Typical Semi-Submersible Platform A more practical approach for providing OTEC power to an oil and gas platform would be to build it into a new platform’s initial design where the OTEC equipment could be more efficiently integrated into the platform design and the electrical system. However, the opportunities for new floating platforms in the GOA are limited as most developments in recent years have been subsea tie-backs to existing platforms rather than new floating platforms. Nonetheless, a new floating platform was recently approved and expected to be producing by 2029 (BP 2024). Though the long-term future is uncertain, one can expect a new floating platform to be built every 1-2 years from now to 2030.1 The synergy of combining OTEC with a production platform is substantial because many of the auxiliary systems that would be required for a stand-alone OTEC facility are already present on a production platform. In some cases, these available systems might need to be expanded to include the OTEC portion (see Table 1). And, of course, the equipment that is dedicated to the OTEC system would be additional to the platform (see Table 2).
